Approved findings

Approved evidence · As of 12 Nov 2026

Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation · paper method: The authors propose keyboard-bound choices and simple annotation tasks, varying option order to reduce priming and showing all alternatives on one screen to avoid scrolling bias.

Permanent record ID: candidate.next8.hovy-lavid.paper.annotation-interface.v1

Approved evidence · As of 12 Nov 2026

Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation · paper method: The paper distinguishes intra-annotator stability over time from inter-annotator reproducibility and discusses simple agreement, Kappa variants and Krippendorff alpha as evaluation measures.

Permanent record ID: candidate.next8.hovy-lavid.paper.annotation-reliability.v1

  • It cautions that high raw agreement can conceal rare-category behavior when the annotation distribution is highly skewed.
  • It argues that acceptable agreement should be set with the corpus intended use in mind.

Approved evidence · As of 12 Nov 2026

Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation · paper method: The paper discusses reconciliation and adjudication of annotation disagreements, cautioning that reconciliation can raise agreement scores while risking overtraining or drift and recommending it mainly for initial training.

Permanent record ID: candidate.next8.hovy-lavid.paper.disagreement-and-adjudication.v2

  • It treats expert adjudication as a consistency-versus-bias tradeoff and leaves open whether adjudicators should see previous annotators’ choices.

Approved evidence · As of 12 Nov 2026

Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation · paper method: The paper proposes an iterative annotation pipeline that selects representative text, instantiates a theory in a codebook, pilots annotation and agreement checks, scales annotation with intermediate checks, and trains and evaluates automation on held-out annotated material.

Permanent record ID: candidate.next8.hovy-lavid.paper.iterative-annotation-pipeline.v1

  • Figure 1 illustrates a 90% agreement gate; the later discussion says acceptable agreement depends on intended use and that 90% is unreachable for many complex problems.
